issues.legal_issue: The limitation period for a declaratory suit begins when the right to sue first accrues, and a later or successive threat does not restart it.
material_facts: In an earlier injunction suit, the respondents expressly asserted that the disputed land belonged to the village commons, had vested in the Central Government after urbanization, and had been transferred to the development authority.
The earlier suit also alleged that officials had threatened to demolish the structures in 1990.

The later declaratory suit was filed in 2000, and the claim that the appellants first learned of the adverse revenue entries in 1998 was inconsistent with their earlier pleadings and the prior written statement.
issues.conclusion: The right to sue first accrued when the appellants knew of the respondents’ unequivocal denial of their claimed rights, and the later declaratory suit was barred by limitation.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3 and Article 58 of the Limitation Act, 1963 require a suit to be dismissed after the prescribed period; Article 58 runs from when the right to sue first accrues. Unlike Article 120 of the Limitation Act, 1908, the word “first” means successive violations do not create a fresh limitation period. The Court applied Mt. Bolo v. Mt. Koklan, Annamalai Chettiar v. A.M.K.C.T. Muthukaruppan Chettiar, Gobinda Narayan Singh v. Sham Lal Singh, and Rukhmabai v. Laxminarayan on accrual of the right to sue upon an effective, clear threat to the asserted right.

predicates.declaratory_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking a declaration of a claimed right.
predicates.prior_clear_denial_of_claim: The opposing party had previously clearly denied the claimant’s asserted right or threatened to infringe it.
predicates.limitation_period_elapsed: The prescribed limitation period had elapsed between the first accrual of the right to sue and commencement of the declaratory suit.

issues.definition: When a declaratory suit follows a prior clear denial of the claim and the prescribed limitation period has elapsed from that first denial, the declaratory claim is time-barred.

issues.legal_issue: Village-commons land that vested in the Central Government upon urbanization could be placed at the development authority’s disposal for its designated purpose.
material_facts: The courts below found that the disputed land belonged to the village commons and that the village had been urbanized.

A government notification placed land that had vested in the Central Government at the development authority’s disposal for development and maintenance as green land, subject to a restriction on construction.
The High Court held, and the Supreme Court found no error in its conclusion, that the land vested in the Central Government and was transferred to the development authority.
issues.conclusion: The finding that the village-commons land vested in the Central Government upon urbanization and was validly placed at the development authority’s disposal was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Section 507(a) of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957, read with Section 150(3) of the Delhi Land Reforms Act, 1954, provides for vesting of village-commons land in the Central Government upon urbanization; Section 22(1) of the Delhi Development Act, 1957, authorizes placing such land at the development authority’s disposal. The Court upheld the High Court’s application of those provisions and referred to Rajinder Kakkar v. Delhi Development Authority.

rule.if: land_ownership_dispute and land_belonged_to_village_commons and rural_area_urbanized and vested_land_transferred_for_designated_purpose

predicates.land_ownership_dispute: The proceeding concerns a dispute over ownership of land.
predicates.land_belonged_to_village_commons: The land was found to belong to the village commons.
predicates.rural_area_urbanized: The rural area in which the land lay was urbanized.
predicates.vested_land_transferred_for_designated_p: The government placed the land that had vested in it at the development authority’s disposal for a stated development or maintenance purpose.

issues.definition: In a land-ownership dispute, when land belonged to the village commons, the rural area was urbanized, and the vested land was transferred for a designated purpose, the land vests in the Central Government and is at the development authority’s disposal.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant seeking title and possessory relief must establish that the land in dispute is the land described in the claimant’s title documents and that the claimant is lawfully entitled to possess it.
material_facts: The appellants produced sale deeds for specified parcels but did not establish the boundaries or location of those parcels with a site plan, demarcation report, or comparable evidence.
The evidence did not connect the site of the restaurant to the parcels described in the sale deeds.
The trial court found that the appellants had not proved lawful possession of the restaurant site, and the Supreme Court upheld that finding.
issues.conclusion: The appellants failed to prove that the restaurant stood on the land they had purchased or that they were lawfully in possession of the disputed site, so their claimed title and possession relief could not succeed.
issues.legal_principle: A claimant asserting title must prove the identity of the land claimed and connect it to the title documents; evidence that a different parcel was purchased does not establish title to the disputed site. The Court upheld the factual finding that the appellants had not made that connection and noted the High Court’s reliance on Rajinder Kakkar v. Delhi Development Authority. The trial court also treated revenue entries such as khasra girdawari as not being documents of title.

predicates.title_and_injunction_suit: The claimant brought a proceeding seeking recognition of title and relief concerning possession of land.
predicates.property_identity_unproved: The claimant did not prove that the disputed site was the parcel identified in the claimant’s title documents.
predicates.lawful_possession_unproved: The claimant did not prove a lawful basis for possessing the disputed site.

issues.definition: In a title-and-injunction suit, if the claimant fails to establish the identity of the land claimed or a lawful basis for possession, the claimed title and possession relief is denied.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant seeking equitable injunctive relief is not entitled to protection after withholding material evidence or undertaking unauthorized construction despite an injunction.
material_facts: The courts found that the appellants withheld material documents, including a site plan, an Aks Sijra, a demarcation report, and an award relating to acquired land.
The appellants raised construction despite an injunction order and without permission from the competent authority.
The Supreme Court approved the finding that the appellants had not approached the court with clean hands.
issues.conclusion: The appellants were not entitled to equitable relief, and the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Injunctive relief is equitable, and a claimant who withholds material facts or documents and acts in disregard of a court order cannot claim that relief. The Court approved the trial court’s finding that the appellants had not approached the court with clean hands and relied on the settled principle that injunction is not granted against the true owner.

predicates.equitable_injunction_proceeding: The claimant sought an injunction as equitable relief.
predicates.material_evidence_withheld: The claimant withheld material facts or documents from the court.
predicates.unauthorized_construction_despite_injunc: The claimant undertook construction without required permission despite an injunction order.

issues.definition: In an equitable injunction proceeding, withholding material evidence or undertaking unauthorized construction despite an injunction results in denial of equitable injunctive relief.
